writings.title: Designing One Clinical Note System for Every Kind of Indian Practice
writings.description: How we designed Nimo's clinical note editor as a block-based system that adapts to allopathy, physiotherapy, Ayurveda, homeopathy, and every other Indian practice type.

blocks.text: The Challenge
Nimo was never meant to be just another allopathy clinic app.

In India, healthcare is not a single workflow. A general physician writes prescriptions and lab orders. A homeopath thinks in case-taking, mentals, generals, particulars, modalities, and remedy rationale. An Ayurvedic doctor may document prakriti, vikriti, pathya, and apathya. A physiotherapist needs assessment, treatment performed, progress tracking, and a home exercise program. Nutritionists, psychologists, naturopaths, dentists, Siddha, Unani, and other practitioners all have their own rhythm.
The real product challenge was this:
How do we design one note-taking system that feels native to every practice type, without building a separate product for each one?

A generic SOAP note would be too rigid. A hospital-style EMR form would become bloated. Separate editors for every system of medicine would be impossible to maintain. We needed a system that could flex with the doctor's practice while staying simple enough for a busy Indian clinic.
The Design Insight
Both of us approached this as designers first.

Our past experience helped. At CureType, we had already seen how healthcare workflows change from specialty to specialty. Irfan's experience in publishing at Conde Nast also shaped the mental model: modern editors are not fixed forms. They are made of blocks.
That became the core design idea:
Treat a clinical note like a block editor, not like a fixed medical form.

Instead of forcing every doctor into the same sequence of fields, Nimo lets the note become a document made of reusable clinical blocks. The doctor can type naturally, then insert the right structured block when needed.
For a prescribing practice, the note can include Vitals, Prescription, Lab, and Follow-up.
For physiotherapy, the note can include Assessment, Treatment performed, Home exercise program, Progress, and Follow-up.
For homeopathy, it can include Case taking.
For Ayurveda, it can include Dosha & Pathya.
The surface stays the same. The blocks change.
Why This Matters in India
Most healthcare software treats "clinic" as one category. That assumption breaks quickly in India.

India has modern medicine, dental, Ayurveda, Homeopathy, Unani, Siddha, Naturopathy, Yoga, Physiotherapy, Psychology, Nutrition, and many hybrid local practices. The diversity is not an edge case. It is the market.
So we designed Nimo around practice type as a first-class product concept. When a clinic signs up, its practice type determines the language, tools, and blocks it sees.

A physiotherapy clinic does not get prescription-heavy screens by default. A homeopath does not have to pretend they are writing an allopathy prescription. An Ayurvedic practitioner gets vocabulary closer to how they actually consult.
This was the designer-first move: we did not start with "what tables do we need?" We started with "what does this doctor need to think clearly during a consultation?"
The System We Built
The final architecture is a single block editor used across practice types.
The editor has a / command, similar to modern writing tools. Doctors can insert blocks as they write. The available menu is resolved from the clinic's practice type.
Option A — a prescribing (allopathy) clinic
Option B — a physiotherapy clinic
At the product level, this gives us three kinds of blocks.
Text blocks are for normal note-taking: headings, paragraphs, and bullet lists.

Content blocks are specialty-specific clinical structures where the content lives inside the note document itself. Examples include Follow-up, Assessment, Treatment performed, Home exercise program, Progress, Case taking, and Dosha & Pathya.

Record blocks appear inside the note but read and write to proper clinical tables. Examples include Prescriptions, Vitals, and Lab orders. These stay connected to the rest of the product: printed prescriptions, pharmacy, billing, lab workflows, patient records, and AI suggestions.

This distinction was important. We wanted the note to feel like one clean document, but we could not flatten critical medical records into plain text. Prescriptions and lab orders needed to remain structured, auditable, printable, and usable elsewhere.
So the design became:
One writing surface. Multiple block types. Structured data where it matters. Freedom where it helps.
The Recording Workflow
We also had to solve the most painful part of clinical documentation: doctors do not have time to write notes during a busy OPD.

Nimo's recording workflow is built into the same editor. The doctor taps Record, speaks naturally during the consultation, and taps Finish notes. Nimo transcribes the visit, generates the note, fills the editor, and keeps the doctor in control to review and edit.
Option A — allopathy
Option B — physiotherapy
The key design decision was to make recording feel like part of note-taking, not a separate AI feature.

The recording dock stays pinned at the bottom of the note. It has clear states: ready, recording, paused, processing, and error. While Nimo processes the audio, the interface shows progress instead of leaving the doctor staring at a blank page. If the note is empty, a ghost scaffold appears so the doctor can see the structure forming.
For longer consultations, recordings can be uploaded in segments. For simpler dictation, the flow stays lightweight. In both cases, the result lands back in the same editor.

We also added trust anchors: the doctor can view the transcript later, copy it, and verify exactly what Nimo heard. The AI draft is never treated as the final truth. It is a starting point. The doctor remains the author.
Bringing Nimo Into the Editor
Once the editor became the centre of the product, AI had a natural place to live.
We did not want Nimo to feel like a separate chatbot or a floating assistant that doctors had to operate. The idea was simpler: Nimo should quietly work around the note.

The doctor records the consultation. Nimo transcribes the conversation, understands the clinical context, and turns it into a structured summary inside the same editor. If the clinic uses templates, Nimo fills the right blocks instead of dumping a wall of text. The doctor can review, edit, and finalise without leaving the note.

For prescribing practices, Nimo can also suggest medicines after the recording. This is especially useful in high-volume clinics where doctors repeat common prescription patterns many times a day. The prescription suggestion appears around the editor, and when accepted, it updates the actual prescription block, not just plain text. That means the prescription can still be printed, used by pharmacy workflows, and stored as structured clinical data.
Option A — allopathy: Nimo suggests a prescription
Option B — physiotherapy: the note Nimo fills
This made the editor more than a writing surface. It became the place where the consultation gets transformed into usable clinical work:

items: speech becomes transcript
transcript becomes summary
summary becomes structured note
clinical context becomes prescription suggestions
final note becomes part of the patient record

blocks.text: The time saved is the obvious benefit. Doctors no longer have to reconstruct the visit at the end of the day or type everything manually during a three-minute consultation.
But the deeper design win is that AI stays in the right role. Nimo prepares the work. The doctor remains in control.
Why This Was a Design Problem First
This work could have easily become an engineering-led settings problem: add more dropdowns, add more templates, add more modules.
Instead, we approached it as a product design problem:

items: What should disappear for a clinic that does not prescribe?
What vocabulary should change for a homeopath or Ayurvedic doctor?
What should remain universal across every doctor?
Which information belongs inside the note, and which must stay as structured medical data?
How can AI help without making the doctor feel out of control?
How can this work on a phone in a crowded Indian clinic?

blocks.text: The answer was not a bigger form. It was a more flexible document.
The Outcome
Nimo now has one note-taking system that adapts to many Indian practice types.
Allopathy and dental clinics get prescriptions, vitals, labs, and follow-up.
Physiotherapy clinics get assessment, treatment, home exercise programs, progress, and follow-up.
Homeopathy gets case-taking.
Ayurveda gets Dosha & Pathya.
Other systems can be added by introducing new blocks, without rebuilding the editor.
We built all of this around the editor, and that is where Nimo came alive: not as a separate AI feature, but as the assistant inside the doctor's daily workflow.
This gives the product a scalable foundation. Every new specialty does not require a new app. It requires understanding the practice deeply enough to design the right blocks.
That is the main story of Nimo: two designers used a publishing-inspired block editor model to solve a healthcare problem that is uniquely Indian in scale and diversity.
We did not design one more clinic note.
We designed a system where every kind of Indian practitioner can feel: this was made for the way I work.

writings.title: I Built a Party Game in 3 Hours. It Crossed 2,000 Rounds in Two Days.
writings.description: What building a small side project with AI taught me about how designers can ship ideas now.

blocks.alt: Three phone screens of Impostor Games: the hub, the Impostor Dance Game home, and a game lobby with animal avatars
blocks.caption: Impostor Games — the hub, the game home, and a lobby mid-join.

blocks.text: Two weeks ago, my family got together for a wedding, and like every family gathering, we ended up looking for games to play.
We wanted to try the viral Impostor Dance Challenge, but none of the existing apps had the Malayalam songs we wanted. Most felt clunky, and many locked content behind a paywall.
Instead of spending more time searching, I opened Claude Code and built a simple version myself.
About three hours later, we were playing.
Everyone had a great time. A few days later, I cleaned up the experience, added a few finishing touches, and published it at impostorgames.com.
The interesting part wasn't building it
The game itself is simple. Most of the effort went into making it feel effortless to play.
No app download.
Every similar game I found lives inside an app. Asking ten people at a party to install something is enough to lose half the room. A web link that opens instantly felt like the better experience.
Join with a QR code.
The host creates a room, everyone scans the QR code, and they're in. No typing room codes. No explaining where to tap next.

blocks.alt: Room created screen with a large QR code and a four-letter room code
blocks.caption: Scan to join — no codes to type, no app to install.

blocks.text: Small details that make waiting fun.
Random animal avatars, a little animation when someone joins, tiny celebratory moments. Nothing groundbreaking, but enough to make the lobby feel less like a waiting room.

blocks.alt: A new player pops into the lobby with a small confetti burst
blocks.caption: The pop-in and confetti burst when a player joins — small enough to feel earned, not shouted.

blocks.text: A consistent visual style.
Warm colours, soft shapes, and a simple design system throughout. I wanted it to feel like a finished product, even if it started as a weekend experiment.
A few days later, my cousin posted a reel featuring the game.
It unexpectedly took off.
Over the last two days alone, people have played more than 2,000 rounds, from over 35 countries.
The numbers were exciting, but they weren't the biggest takeaway for me.
What stayed with me was how quickly an idea went from, “Wouldn't it be nice if this existed?” to something that thousands of people were actually using.
Why I wanted to share this
I think we're entering a really exciting time for designers.
Not because AI replaces design, but because it removes so many of the barriers between having an idea and putting it in front of people.
You no longer need to wait until you know how to code everything yourself. You can prototype, build, test, and ship much faster than before.
The tools help us build.
But the experience still comes from us—the decisions we make, the details we obsess over, and the care we put into every interaction.
If you've been sitting on an idea for a while, this might be the best time to build it.

writings.title: Spacing components in Design Systems
writings.description: On building consistent, scalable spacing systems for components — and why most teams get it backwards.

blocks.text: Spacing might seem simple, but it’s one of the most powerful tools in creating clear, consistent, and visually balanced interfaces. In design systems, however, managing spacing—especially for reusable components, often turns into a frustrating puzzle for designers and developers alike. So how do we keep things consistent without sacrificing flexibility? This article explores key principles to consider when defining spacing for components in a design system.
Understanding Spacing: Margin vs. Padding
Before we delve into best practices, it's essential to clarify two core concepts:
Margin

items: What it is: Margin is the space outside an element.
Purpose: It defines the space between that element and adjacent elements.
Use case: Often used to create separation between components at the layout level.

blocks.text: Padding

items: What it is: Padding is the space inside an element.
Purpose: It defines the space between the element’s content and its border.
Use case: Should be used to provide breathing room inside components, especially when they have a background color or border

blocks.text: Avoid Outer Spacing in Reusable Components

One of the most common mistakes in design systems is assigning outer spacing (margin/padding) to reusable components. While it might seem convenient at first, this approach often leads to layout rigidity and inconsistency.

blocks.caption: An example when a card component has a fixed margin built into it, placing multiple cards within a new layout—like a grid or list—can lead to unintended extra spacing. Since the margin is baked into the card itself, it becomes difficult for the parent layout to control or adjust spacing between cards, often resulting in inconsistent gaps or layout misalignment.

blocks.text: Important Guideline Avoid using padding unless the element has a background or border. Padding makes sense only when it helps define the visual bounds of a component.
Why Outer Spacing is Problematic

items: Unpredictable Layouts: Components with built-in margins push against each other or their containers, making layout behavior harder to predict.
Lack of Flexibility: The same component may need different spacing depending on its placement or context.
Difficult Overrides: Margins defined within components are often hard to override cleanly at the parent level.

blocks.text: Embrace Layout-Driven Spacing
The preferred strategy is to remove all outer spacing from reusable components and define spacing only at the layout (or parent) level.
Use gap for Layout Spacing

Modern CSS offers the gap property, which is ideal for managing spacing between elements within a container. It provides a cleaner, more intuitive, and maintainable approach compared to manually setting margins on individual elements. It closely mirrors how designers define spacing between layers in tools like Figma.

items: Works with flex, grid, and multi-column layouts.
Eliminates the need for “last-child” margin hacks.
Keeps the component logic simple and reusable.

blocks.text: Benefits of Layout-Based Spacing
1. Greater Spacing Flexibility
By centralizing spacing at the layout level, you can:

items: Adjust spacing based on screen size or context.
Apply spacing tokens dynamically based on design needs.
Create reusable layout containers (e.g., stacks or insets) that enforce spacing rules.

blocks.text: 2. Component Reusability
A single component can be used in multiple contexts without having to redefine or override its spacing behavior. This keeps components truly atomic and portable.
3. Cleaner Code and Token Usage
Using spacing tokens at the layout level ensures consistent rhythm across the system. It also makes it easier for designers and developers to reason about space relationships.
Handling Complex Components
What about components that require dynamic spacing internally—those that change based on conditionally rendered sub-elements?

Take the example of a Story Card component, which can include elements like a rubric, title, description, byline, and date. If spacing is managed using fixed margins and padding, enabling or disabling these elements could cause the internal spacing to shift unpredictably.
The example above illustrates how the outer spacing of the same Story Card shifts when different combinations of elements are toggled on or off through component properties.
Structure First, Then Space

One easy way to space elements within complex components, apply Gestalt’s Law of Proximity to guide grouping. Elements placed closer together are perceived as related. This principle helps inform both the structure of the component and the thoughtful use of gap between groups.

The example above shows how internal spacing within the same Story Card can be managed using gap (space-between) instead of fixed padding or margins. With gap, the spacing isn’t tied to any specific element—it exists only between elements. This means if an element is removed, the corresponding space automatically disappears, keeping the layout clean and consistent.

items: Group related elements: Identify which sub-elements are visually and functionally connected, and wrap them in internal layout containers (e.g., vertical stacks, horizontal groups). Use gap to create consistent spacing within these groups.
Use padding only when needed: Apply padding inside a component only when it has a background color or border to create internal breathing room.
Avoid fixed margins: Do not define external margins within components. Allow the parent layout to control spacing between components for better flexibility and consistency.

blocks.text: Conclusion

Designing scalable spacing in a design system starts with the separation of component structure and layout responsibility. Components should focus on their own internal alignment and content padding, leaving external spacing to the parent layout.
By using modern CSS tools like gap and adopting layout-driven spacing strategies, your design system can gain:

items: Consistency
Flexibility
Maintainability

blocks.text: This results in cleaner components, fewer overrides, and a smoother collaboration between design and engineering.

writings.title: Improving Accessibility for Overlay Cards in Verso
writings.description: How we improved the contrast and readability of overlay cards in Verso without sacrificing the brand's visual character.

blocks.text: The Overlay Story Card is a widely used design pattern across multiple brands including Vogue, Bon Appétit, GQ and Traveller. It has an image background with a dark gradient overlay, topped with a story title, metadata, and sometimes a byline. It’s a visually engaging layout, but without careful attention to contrast, alignment, and image balance, it can harm accessibility and usability.
This article explains how I identified key problems, what changes we made, and the color contrast theory that informed those changes.
The Problem
The Overlay Story Card is a design pattern where a story title and details are placed on top of an image with a black gradient overlay.
In the current implementation:

items: The background overlay takes fixed height from bottom, fading from 80% black to 0% from bottom to a fixed height.
This style is used in several recirculation list and story collection components across our brands.

blocks.text: However, during an accessibility review, it became clear that critical improvements were needed.
My role

My role was to identify the accessibility gaps, propose a solution for improving text legibility, and work closely with design and engineering teams to bring the changes into the Verso Design System. I ensured the final implementation balanced accessibility standards with the visual expression of brands like Vogue, Bon Appétit, and GQ.
Identifying the Issues
1. Legibility Problems
On smaller screens, the gradient fades too quickly, reducing opacity near the top.

Since the story title gets placed towards the top/middle of the image, the text often overlaps with lighter areas of the background image, making it harder to read and failing accessibility contrast checks.
2. Image Visibility Loss
The rubric, title, and byline collectively cover more than half of the image, which hides too much of the visual content and reduces its impact.
3. Content Scannability
Center-aligned text interrupts natural reading flow. Each new line forces the reader to pause and find the starting point, slowing down scanning speed.
Approach to Fixing It

The initial proposal was to replace the overlay approach with a stacked card design. This would have eliminated all of the accessibility issues we identified. However, maintaining the visual language was critical—our brands needed the solution to stay closely aligned with their established identity. So we explored alternative solutions that would address accessibility issues while preserving the brand’s visual expression and user experience.

We ran the numbers to understand how to eliminate the accessibility issue. Since the lightest possible background in an image can be pure white, we used that as the baseline for testing. If white text can achieve sufficient contrast on top of pure white with an overlay, it will be legible on any other surface as well.

For white text (#FFFFFF) to meet WCAG AA (4.5:1) against a pure white background (#FFFFFF), a black overlay of at least 53.47% opacity is required. To meet the stricter WCAG AAA (7:1) standard, the overlay must be at least 65.08% opacity.
The problem with the old gradient was that it faded too quickly to lower opacity levels, making it impossible to consistently guarantee these contrast thresholds wherever text appeared.
1. Gradient Overlay Applied to Text Layer
To ensure white text consistently meets accessibility guidelines, we refined how gradients were applied:

items: Instead of relying on the card’s fixed background, the gradient was applied directly to the text layer wrap.
This made the gradient independent of text height, ensuring both short and long headlines remain equally readable.
Within the text wrap, the gradient now ranges from 90% to 55% black, guaranteeing white text always passes WCAG AA contrast standards.
On top of this, we added a fixed gradient from 55% to 0%, preserving the smooth visual fade while maintaining legibility.

blocks.caption: An illustration showing how the new implementation works

blocks.text: 2. Increased Image Ratio
We recommended brands to use image height for mobile and tablet breakpoints by shifting the aspect ratio to atleast 1:1. This would more be a brand decision based on their text length.
This allows more of the image to be visible, improving visual storytelling without sacrificing legibility.
3. Left-Aligned Content
All overlay text is now left-aligned to improve scanning.
This aligns with common reading patterns, allowing users to quickly find the start of each new line without extra visual effort.

blocks.caption: Screenshots from Vogue and Bon Appétit showcasing the updated design changes

blocks.text: Outcome
By rethinking the gradient application, adjusting the image ratio, and improving text alignment, the Overlay Story Card is now:

items: Accessible across devices and image types
Visually balanced with improved image visibility
Faster to scan and read, enhancing the overall user experience
